en: The Sutra on the Profound and Great Dedication Spoken by the Buddha.
In the *Monk You’s Catalog*, the translator’s name was lost; it is now appended to the Song Dynasty catalog.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the great multitude before and behind him, was preaching the Dharma.

Then, within the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Mingtian (Clear Wisdom), who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to ask a question; I only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain it for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mingtian:
“Good son! If you wish to ask anything, do not hesitate; the Tathāgata shall explain it for you according to your questions.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mingtian addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it that a bodhisattva cultivates few roots of goodness yet obtains a great fruit, or performs many meritorious deeds yet receives immeasurable rewards?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mingtian:
“Excellent, excellent!”
Excellent! It is well that you are able to inquire about such a meaning before the Buddha.

You have already planted many roots of merit under immeasurable Buddhas of the past, made offerings to those Buddhas, and drawn near to spiritual friends; thus, for the sake of sentient beings who delight in merit, you are able to pose this profoundly deep question.
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
The Bodhisattva Mingtian addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mingtian:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, in the presence of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, cultivate bodily conduct of loving-kindness, verbal conduct of loving-kindness, and mental conduct of loving-kindness, single-mindedly recollecting the meritorious deeds performed by those Buddhas.”
Furthermore, Bright One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should go to the honored temples of the Tathāgata to pay homage and make offerings. Kneeling on the right knee with palms joined, they should circumambulate them to the right, scattering flowers and burning incense, hanging silken banners and canopies, and performing various musical performances with reverence and respect. With subtle and wondrous voices and profound words and meanings, they should praise the Buddha’s merits, rejoicing in and extolling his excellence.
The Buddha told Mingtian:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in the presence of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, cultivate the practice of loving-kindness through body, cultivate the practice of loving-kindness through speech, and cultivate the practice of loving-kindness through mind, while recollecting the merits of the Buddhas?"

"Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should contemplate the Tathāgata as the steadfast one, the unsurpassed one, the most excellent one; as a lion king, courageous and fearless; who saves himself and saves others, brings peace to himself and brings peace to others, attains extinction himself and leads others to extinction; who proclaims the Dharma of ultimate truth to establish sentient beings; whose mind is free from flattery and artifice and who is fully endowed with pure precepts; whose powers, fearlessnesses, and eloquence have forever eliminated all obstructions and habitual tendencies; and who is sovereign over the Dharma, with no equal."

Having thus single-mindedly contemplated the merit of the Buddha’s mindfulness, one places the right knee upon the ground and makes offerings of scattered flowers, burning incense, banners, silken streamers, canopies, and music; this is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of compassionate physical action.
To praise the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata with subtle and wondrous songs and profound words and meanings is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of compassionate verbal action.
Because of those roots of goodness in body and speech, to mindfully contemplate the Buddha’s merit with utmost sincerity and reverence is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of compassionate mental action.
"Tomorrow!
Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, in the presence of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, cultivates loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind, and practices right mindfulness.
The Buddha again addressed Mingtian:

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, toward all sentient beings of the past, future, and present, should likewise cultivate compassionate conduct of body, cultivate compassionate conduct of speech, and cultivate compassionate conduct of mind, maintaining equanimous mindfulness toward all sentient beings."

Mañjuśrī, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate compassionate conduct of body, speech, and mind toward sentient beings of the three periods of time, maintaining an impartial mindfulness toward all beings?
Thus it is, Bright One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not kill living beings, does not steal the wealth of others, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, does not engage in frivolous speech, does not engage in divisive speech, does not engage in harsh speech, does not harbor covetousness, does not harbor ill will, and does not hold wrong views.
How does a bodhisattva refrain from killing sentient beings?
They regard all sentient beings with compassion and affection, possessing a sense of shame and remorse, and forever relinquish the sword and staff.
Regarding non-stealing: whether in a village or a deserted place, they do not take what has been left behind without it being given.

As for one who refrains from sexual misconduct: if a woman has a protector—whether protected by her parents, brothers, or kinsmen—one does not give rise to thoughts of desire even upon seeing her receive a single stalk of a flower.
Regarding non-false speech: whether in a village or before a king where one is called upon to serve as a witness, one speaks with sincere truth and would rather die than speak falsely.

Regarding non-divisive speech: one always maintains a sense of harmony between those parties; what one hears from that side, one does not repeat to this side, and what one hears from this side, one does not repeat to that side.
One who refrains from harsh speech uses gentle words, provides instruction and exhortation, and greets others with kindness; they never inflict bitter or malicious words upon sentient beings.

One who refrains from frivolous speech speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks with knowledge of the meaning, and speaks for the benefit of others, ensuring there is no discrepancy between their mind and their words.
One who is free from greed does not give rise to thoughts of desire regarding the wealth and profit of others; upon seeing someone come to take it, their mind is free of stinginess.

One who is free from anger eliminates all resentment toward all sentient beings, giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, a mind of benefit, and a mind that pacifies others, thereby harmoniously gathering and sustaining all sentient beings.

One who is free from wrong view holds that there is giving, there is sacrifice, there is offering; there are parents; there are this world and the next world; there are fruits and results of good and evil deeds; and that in the world there are Arhats who, having realized it for themselves through direct knowledge, declare: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I myself know that there will be no further existence."
"O Bright One! You should know that when he does not kill, does not steal, and does not engage in sexual misconduct, this is the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of compassionate physical conduct;
when he does not engage in false speech, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech, this is the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of compassionate verbal conduct."
To be free from greed, free from malice, and free from wrong views constitutes the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the mental practice of loving-kindness;
to cultivate loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind constitutes the bodhisattva’s impartial regard for all sentient beings.
The Buddha told Mingtian:

"A Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in the presence of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, cultivates compassionate conduct of body, compassionate conduct of speech, and compassionate conduct of mind; and toward all sentient beings of the past, future, and present, he likewise cultivates compassionate conduct of body, compassionate conduct of speech, and compassionate conduct of mind. He shares all the merit and retribution thereof with all sentient beings and dedicates it toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Excellent!

When a bodhisattva performs such dedication, this is called a bodhisattva obtaining a great fruit and reward from cultivating even a small amount of the roots of goodness; having performed much merit, their blessed rewards will be immeasurable."
The Buddha told Mingtian:

"When this bodhisattva accomplishes immeasurable merit, he dedicates that merit toward immeasurable wisdom; furthermore, together with all sentient beings, he dedicates it entirely toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
These three kinds of merit have three kinds of dedication.
What are the three? They are:

the emptiness of the past, the emptiness of the future, and the emptiness of the present. There is no one who dedicates, there is no dharma of dedication, and there is no place of dedication; the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should perform dedication in this manner.
When performing this dedication, all three spheres are pure; one shares these pure merits with all sentient beings and dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

One who performs such dedication does not perceive ordinary beings or the dharmas of ordinary beings; nor do they perceive those who practice through faith or those who practice through dharma; nor do they perceive the eight types of persons; nor do they perceive stream-enterers or those approaching the fruit of stream-entry; nor do they perceive once-returners or those approaching the fruit of once-returning; nor do they perceive non-returners or those approaching the fruit of non-returning; nor do they perceive arhats or those approaching the fruit of arhatship; nor do they perceive pratyekabuddhas or those approaching the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood; nor do they perceive buddhas or those approaching buddhahood.
Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without conditions, neither arising nor ceasing, and has no place of abiding.

Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should, by means of these three kinds of dedication and three kinds of pure merit, share them with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having performed this dedication, the bodhisattva further makes this vow:

"In whatever place I am born, may I always encounter all Buddhas; may I attain profound samādhi and behold immeasurable Buddhas; may I accomplish extensive learning and pure wisdom; and may I never abandon any sentient being through my great vows."
When this Dharma was being taught, hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all aspired to be reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"When I previously taught this profound Dharma, hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all aspired to be reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha."

Ānanda, you should know that when they pass away from this life, they shall all be reborn in the Land of Wonderful Joy in the presence of Akṣobhya Buddha. From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they will make offerings to the various Buddhas and listen to the true Dharma; they will attain dhāraṇīs and practice according to the teachings, and they shall all achieve inconceivable wisdom. In lands of the five turbidities, they shall all become Buddhas, all bearing the same name: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha King of Ambrosia Sound (Amṛtaghoṣarāja).
"You should know that when that deva received this prediction, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should know that this is a path of great merit, of immeasurable merit,
and of boundless merit. The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
"Because this Dharma is ultimately pure.
"World-Honored One,
by what name should this sutra be called?"
"How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!"
"This sutra is titled 'The Great Dedication' and is also titled 'The Dedication of the Profound Nature of Phenomena';
you should uphold it. The Buddha told Kauśika:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who study this dedication, you should know that these persons will surely attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), will be able to deliver those not yet delivered, and will bring peace and happiness to hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings."
When this Dharma was thus spoken, the assembly of bhikṣus, the Śakras, Brahmās, devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Profound and Great Dedication Spoken by the Buddha.
